questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying the distribution of potassium between body compartments, summarized in the diagram below. Which of the following best explains why small shifts of K+ between compartments produce disproportionately large changes in plasma [K+]?
questions.diagram:
Potassium distribution and balance
Total body K+: ~3,500 mEq (≈50 mEq/kg lean mass)
~98% intracellular (ICF [K+] ≈ 140 mEq/L)
~2% extracellular (ECF [K+] ≈ 4 mEq/L)
Daily intake ≈ 100 mEq → ~90% renal, ~10% GI excretion
Plasma [K+] is set by: (1) cellular shift (ICF↔ECF) and (2) renal excretion
choices: The narrow ECF compartment magnifies any ICF→ECF shift
K+ is freely filtered at the glomerulus
The kidney rapidly compensates for any change
Insulin always restores K+ within 5 minutes
explanations: Correct. ~98% of total body K+ is intracellular (ICF [K+] ≈ 140 mEq/L); the ECF holds only ~2%. The disproportion means that small shifts of K+ between ICF and ECF — driven by insulin, β-adrenergic activity, acid-base status, aldosterone, or cell lysis — produce large changes in plasma [K+] WITHOUT measurable change in total body K+. Conversely, total body K+ may be markedly depleted (e.g., chronic diarrhea, DKA) yet plasma K+ may appear normal or even elevated because of competing cellular shifts. Plasma K+ is therefore a poor index of total body K+.
Incorrect. Filtration at the glomerulus is freely permitted but is not the explanation for plasma K+ sensitivity to shifts.
Incorrect. Renal compensation occurs over hours-to-days, not the minutes in which a cellular shift can change plasma K+.
Incorrect. Insulin DOES drive K+ shift into cells, but the question is about the structural reason that small shifts produce big plasma changes.
Incorrect. Aldosterone regulates renal K+ excretion (over hours-to-days); minute-to-minute plasma K+ stability depends largely on the cellular shift mechanisms.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents in DKA. Initial plasma K+ is 5.5 mEq/L. After 2 hours of intravenous insulin and fluid resuscitation, plasma K+ has fallen to 3.8 mEq/L — though total body K+ has not appreciably changed in this short interval. Which of the following best explains the rapid fall in plasma K+?
choices: Insulin acutely increases urinary K+ excretion
Insulin activates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting K+ into cells
Insulin reduces intestinal absorption of K+
Insulin destroys K+ through enzymatic degradation
explanations: Incorrect. Insulin's principal effect on plasma K+ is cellular shift, not enhanced urinary excretion (renal K+ excretion is largely set by aldosterone and distal Na+ delivery).

Correct. Insulin binds its tyrosine kinase receptor and activates skeletal muscle (and other cell membrane) Na+/K+-ATPase, accelerating Na+ extrusion and K+ uptake into cells. Plasma K+ falls within 15–30 minutes by ~0.5–1.0 mEq/L through redistribution; total body K+ is unchanged in the short term (although in DKA renal K+ losses from osmotic diuresis continue separately). This is exploited therapeutically in hyperkalemia (insulin + glucose), and explains why K+ supplementation is added to DKA fluids when plasma K+ falls below ~5.0.
Incorrect. Insulin does not chemically chelate K+.
Incorrect. Insulin does not reduce intestinal K+ absorption.
Incorrect. Insulin does not destroy K+; the change in plasma K+ is purely a redistribution between compartments.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with severe asthma is treated with continuous nebulized albuterol. Three hours later his plasma K+ has fallen from 4.0 to 3.2 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains the fall in plasma K+?
choices: Albuterol increases urinary K+ excretion via a direct renal effect
Albuterol activates Na+/K+-ATPase via β2/cAMP, shifting K+ into cells
explanations: Incorrect. β2 agonists do not principally raise renal K+ excretion; the mechanism is cellular shift.
Incorrect. β2 agonists do not affect intestinal K+ absorption.

Correct. β2-adrenergic receptor activation on skeletal muscle stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase via Gs-coupled cAMP signaling. The pump drives K+ from ECF into cells, lowering plasma K+ by ~0.5 mEq/L within 15–30 minutes. In hyperkalemia, high-dose nebulized albuterol (10–20 mg, much higher than asthma dosing) provides a temporizing K+-lowering effect alongside insulin/glucose. Note: this mechanism explains why iatrogenic hypokalemia is not uncommon during high-dose β2 therapy for asthma.
Incorrect. Albuterol does not chelate plasma K+.
Incorrect. Albuterol does not produce osmotic diuresis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents in DKA with severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.10, HCO3− 8 mEq/L) and plasma K+ 5.6 mEq/L. He is known to be total-body K+ depleted from osmotic diuresis. Which of the following best explains the elevated plasma K+ despite total body K+ depletion?
choices: Acidosis only occurs in the setting of hypokalemia
Acidosis-driven H+/K+ exchange combined with insulin deficiency raises plasma K+
Acidosis lowers plasma K+ by direct renal effect
explanations: Incorrect. Acidosis tends to LOWER aldosterone-driven distal K+ secretion (because H+ secretion competes with K+ secretion at α-intercalated cells), not increase it.
Incorrect. Aldosterone synthesis is not selectively upregulated by acidosis.
Incorrect. Acidosis can occur with hyper- OR hypokalemia, depending on cause.

Correct. Acidosis-induced hyperkalemia is most pronounced in MINERAL acid acidoses where the conjugate anion (Cl−) cannot accompany H+ into cells, forcing exchange with intracellular K+. In organic acidoses (DKA, lactic acidosis), the conjugate anion (β-hydroxybutyrate, lactate) accompanies H+ across membranes, blunting the K+ shift. In DKA, the dominant cause of apparent hyperkalemia is INSULIN DEFICIENCY (loss of Na+/K+-ATPase stimulation), with acidosis playing a smaller role. Insulin therapy reveals the underlying total body K+ deficit.
Incorrect. Acidosis does not lower plasma K+; it raises plasma K+ via the cellular shift mechanism described.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is started on induction chemotherapy for newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma. Eight hours after the first dose, she develops weakness, vomiting, and ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS). Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Tumor lysis syndrome with massive cellular release of K+, PO4, urate
explanations: Incorrect. AKI is part of the picture but does not explain the hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia together.
Incorrect. The clinical picture and lab profile do not match drug-induced aldosterone resistance.
Incorrect. The acidosis is mild; the dominant mechanism is direct cellular release.
Incorrect. Heparin would not be the relevant mechanism in this clinical setting.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) results from rapid death of malignant cells releasing their intracellular contents — K+, phosphate, uric acid, and LDH — into the bloodstream. The high phosphate complexes with calcium (precipitating in tissues), producing hypocalcemia. Uric acid crystallizes in renal tubules causing urate nephropathy and AKI. Hyperkalemia is the most immediately life-threatening feature. Risk factors: high-grade lymphomas (Burkitt), AML/ALL with high WBC, bulky disease, high LDH. Prevention: aggressive hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase before chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old marine recruit collapses during heat training and is found to have CK 75,000 U/L, plasma K+ 6.5 mEq/L, and tea-colored urine. The hyperkalemia is attributed in part to the underlying muscle injury. Which of the following best explains the contribution of rhabdomyolysis to hyperkalemia?
choices: Direct release of intracellular K+ from injured myocytes
Massive insulin release shifts K+ out of cells
Aldosterone deficiency due to adrenal injury
explanations: Correct. Rhabdomyolysis releases the intracellular contents of injured myocytes — K+ (which is concentrated ~140 mEq/L in cells vs ~4 in plasma), phosphate, myoglobin, creatine, uric acid, LDH, and others. Plasma K+ rises both from this direct cellular release and from concurrent AKI (myoglobin-induced ATN reduces renal K+ excretion). The hyperphosphatemia and uric acid/AKI overlap with the picture of tumor lysis syndrome.
Incorrect. Insulin shifts K+ INTO cells, lowering plasma K+. There is no massive insulin release in rhabdomyolysis.
Incorrect. Heparin is not a feature of routine rhabdomyolysis presentation.
Incorrect. Adrenal injury is not a typical feature of rhabdomyolysis from heat illness.
Incorrect. Stress catecholamines β2-stimulate (rather than block) Na+/K+-ATPase, which would tend to LOWER plasma K+, not raise it.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying the renal handling of potassium. Most filtered K+ is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb. Which of the following segments is the principal site of REGULATED K+ secretion that ultimately determines urinary K+ excretion?
choices: Cortical and outer medullary collecting duct (CCD/OMCD)
explanations: Incorrect. The PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered K+ paracellularly with water, but is not the regulated secretion site.

Correct. While most filtered K+ is reabsorbed in the PCT (~65%) and TAL (~25%), the urinary K+ excretion is principally set by REGULATED secretion in the cortical and outer medullary collecting duct. Aldosterone-stimulated principal cells secrete K+ via apical ROMK (constitutive) and BK channels (flow-activated). Four major variables determine the rate of K+ secretion: (1) plasma K+ (direct stimulus to aldosterone), (2) aldosterone level, (3) distal Na+ delivery (substrate for ENaC, which creates the lumen-negative voltage), and (4) urine flow rate (washes K+ away from the apical membrane, maintaining the gradient).
Incorrect. The thin descending limb is not a major site of K+ transport.
Incorrect. The TAL reabsorbs ~25% of filtered K+ via NKCC2, but is not the regulated secretion site.
Incorrect. Bowman capsule is a filtration site, not a transport site.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) has elevated aldosterone and serum K+ of 2.9 mEq/L due to renal K+ wasting. Which of the following combination of factors most directly drives K+ secretion at the principal cell?
choices: Decreased apical Na+ entry via ENaC and decreased urine flow
Hypokalemia and high renal blood flow
Aldosterone, distal Na+ delivery, urine flow rate, and high plasma K+
explanations: Incorrect. Decreased ENaC and low urine flow REDUCE K+ secretion; the question asks what DRIVES it.
Incorrect. High RBF does not directly drive K+ secretion; the relevant variable is distal flow at the principal cell, not glomerular flow.

Correct. Distal K+ secretion is driven by four mutually amplifying factors: (1) aldosterone (via mineralocorticoid receptor → ENaC, ROMK, Na+/K+-ATPase); (2) high distal Na+ delivery (more Na+ available for ENaC reabsorption, creating a more lumen-negative voltage that drives K+ out); (3) high urine flow (washes secreted K+ away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient and opening flow-activated BK channels); and (4) high plasma K+ (a direct stimulus to aldosterone secretion AND to ROMK trafficking). All four are present in Conn syndrome and converge to produce the characteristic hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Reduced Na+/K+-ATPase activity would impair K+ uptake into the principal cell and reduce K+ secretion.
Incorrect. Bowman-space pressure relates to filtration, not distal K+ secretion.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic heart failure on furosemide develops hypokalemia (K+ 2.9). Which of the following mechanisms contributes most to renal K+ wasting in patients on loop diuretic therapy?
choices: Direct K+-pump inhibition by furosemide at the principal cell
Increased distal Na+ delivery, urine flow, and aldosterone amplify K+ secretion
explanations: Incorrect. Furosemide acts at NKCC2 in the TAL, not directly on the principal cell K+ pump.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not reduce filtered K+ load.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics INCREASE aldosterone (via volume contraction), which compounds K+ wasting.

Correct. Loop diuretics produce hypokalemia through three amplifying mechanisms acting at the principal cell: (1) increased distal Na+ delivery (TAL Na+ reabsorption is blocked, so more Na+ reaches the collecting duct, fueling ENaC); (2) increased urine flow rate (washes secreted K+ away from the apical membrane and activates BK channels); and (3) volume contraction-mediated RAAS activation (high aldosterone). The same triad explains thiazide-induced hypokalemia. Concomitant K+ supplementation, K+-sparing diuretics, or aldosterone antagonists are commonly used to prevent or treat the hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not increase intestinal K+ absorption.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old physiologist is studying potassium handling at the principal cell of the cortical collecting duct. Beyond the constitutive ROMK channel, principal cells express a flow-activated K+ channel that opens with apical membrane stretch. Which of the following best identifies this channel?
explanations: Incorrect. ROMK is one of two principal-cell K+ channels; BK is the other (flow-activated).
Incorrect. Na+/K+-ATPase is basolateral and pumps K+ into the cell; it is not an apical secretion channel.
Incorrect. ENaC is the apical Na+ channel of principal cells (a different ion).
Incorrect. AQP2 is the apical water channel.

Correct. Principal cells express two apical K+ channels: ROMK (constitutive, mediates baseline K+ secretion) and BK (large-conductance Ca2+-activated, flow-activated). BK opens in response to apical membrane stretch from increased tubular flow, providing a 'flow reserve' of K+ secretion above what ROMK alone provides. This explains why high urine flow rate (e.g., osmotic diuresis from glycosuria, loop diuretics, post-obstructive diuresis) drives K+ wasting independent of aldosterone — and why aldosterone-independent K+ losses can be substantial when distal flow is high.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea has persistent hypokalemia (K+ 2.7) despite oral KCl 80 mEq/day. Serum magnesium is 1.0 mg/dL (low). Which of the following best explains why her hypokalemia is refractory to K+ replacement?
choices: KCl is being absorbed but excreted unchanged in the urine
Hypomagnesemia removes Mg2+ inhibition of ROMK, driving K+ wasting
Mg2+ deficiency affects only neuromuscular function
K+ replacement should simply be dosed higher; Mg+ status is irrelevant
explanations: Incorrect. The mechanism is renal K+ wasting from inappropriate ROMK activity, not GI loss of administered KCl.

Correct. ROMK channels in principal cells are normally closed by intracellular Mg2+ binding to the inner pore (Mg2+ block). In hypomagnesemia, intracellular Mg2+ falls and the Mg2+ block is lost — ROMK remains 'open' inappropriately, allowing K+ to leak into the lumen and be excreted even when plasma K+ is low. Until Mg2+ is repleted, K+ supplementation simply 'feeds' this ongoing renal K+ wasting. This is a well-documented clinical phenomenon: hypokalemia refractory to K+ replacement requires assessment and correction of magnesium.
Incorrect. Mg2+ does not chemically chelate K+.
Incorrect. Hypomagnesemia has multiple effects, including this critical effect on renal K+ handling.
Incorrect. Mg+ status is HIGHLY relevant; failure to address it is the most common reason for refractory hypokalemia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with longstanding type 2 diabetes mellitus has serum K+ 5.7 mEq/L, mild metabolic acidosis (HCO3− 18, anion gap normal), urine pH 5.0, low plasma renin activity, and low plasma aldosterone. Which of the following best characterizes this disorder?
choices: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemic alkalosis
Type 2 (proximal) RTA with Fanconi syndrome features
explanations: Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features HYPOkalemic alkalosis with inability to acidify urine (urine pH ≥5.5) — opposite to this profile.
Incorrect. Type 2 RTA features hypokalemia and is associated with Fanconi syndrome.

Correct. Type 4 RTA in diabetes is most commonly due to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism: chronic intrarenal injury reduces JG cell renin secretion, lowering aldosterone. Reduced aldosterone impairs distal Na+ reabsorption, K+ secretion, and downstream H+ secretion (because intracellular acidosis from hyperkalemia further impairs ammoniagenesis). The result is hyperkalemia, mild hyperchloremic non-anion-gap acidosis, with NORMAL distal acidification (the H+-ATPase machinery itself is intact). Treatment: dietary K+ restriction, loop diuretics, fludrocortisone in selected cases, and avoiding ACE inhibitors/ARBs/spironolactone where possible.
Incorrect. Lactic acidosis features ELEVATED anion gap; this patient's gap is normal.
Incorrect. DKA features ketosis with elevated anion gap and hyperglycemia.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with chronic systolic heart failure has been on stable lisinopril and spironolactone for two years. One week ago she started ibuprofen for knee osteoarthritis. She now presents with profound muscle weakness, palpitations, and ECG showing peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Laboratory studies are shown.

labs.name: ECG
labs.value: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, flattened P waves

choices: Tumor lysis syndrome from occult malignancy
Combined ACE inhibitor + spironolactone + NSAID hyperkalemia
explanations: Incorrect. Hemolysis would show indirect hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, and elevated LDH — not described here.
Incorrect. TLS would feature hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia in addition to hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. The mild HCO3− decrease is far too small to explain a K+ rise from baseline to 7.4.

Correct. The 'triple threat' of ACE inhibitor (or ARB) + spironolactone (or eplerenone) + NSAID converges on distal K+ secretion: the ACE inhibitor lowers AT II → lowers aldosterone; spironolactone blocks the MR; the NSAID reduces afferent prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation, lowering GFR and reducing distal Na+ delivery. Each impairs K+ secretion individually; together they can produce life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in elderly patients with HF and reduced renal function. Recognition prompts withdrawal of the offending drugs (the NSAID is usually the easiest to stop), and treatment of the hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on continuous IV heparin for 5 days for a pulmonary embolism develops hyperkalemia (K+ 5.8). Renal function is unchanged. Which of the following best explains heparin-induced hyperkalemia?
choices: Heparin stimulates β2 receptors and shifts K+
explanations: Correct. Heparin (both unfractionated and low-molecular-weight) inhibits aldosterone synthesis at the zona glomerulosa, with effects on aldosterone synthase and on the cells themselves with prolonged use. The fall in aldosterone reduces distal K+ secretion, raising plasma K+. This effect is more pronounced with prolonged exposure and in patients who are otherwise predisposed to aldosterone deficiency (renal impairment, diabetes, RAAS inhibitor use). Stopping heparin generally allows aldosterone secretion to recover; severe hyperkalemia may require additional measures.
Incorrect. Heparin does not chelate plasma K+.
Incorrect. Heparin does not produce osmotic diuresis.
Incorrect. Heparin does not stimulate β2 receptors.
Incorrect. Heparin does not activate ENaC; the lesion is upstream at the adrenal cortex.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease who missed her dialysis session presents with palpitations and weakness. Her serum potassium is 7.5 mEq/L. The ECG shows characteristic findings of moderately severe hyperkalemia. Which row in the table best describes the typical ECG progression at this serum K+ level?
explanations: Incorrect. Peaked, narrow T waves with otherwise normal ECG describe MILD hyperkalemia (~5.5–6.5 mEq/L); P waves remain present and QRS is normal width.

Correct. At moderate hyperkalemia (~6.5–7.5), peaked T waves are joined by P-wave flattening (and PR prolongation) and QRS widening — reflecting progressive impairment of intra-atrial and intraventricular conduction. As K+ rises further (>8), P waves disappear and the QRS broadens further into a sine wave — preceding cardiac arrest. The progression is roughly: peaked T → flattened P + wide QRS → absent P + sine wave.
Incorrect. Sine-wave morphology with absent P waves describes SEVERE hyperkalemia (>8 mEq/L) — pre-arrest.
Incorrect. Flattened T waves with U waves describe HYPOkalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. T-wave inversion is associated with ischemia or strain pattern, not hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with end-stage renal disease and missed dialysis has K+ 7.8 with peaked T waves and widened QRS on ECG. The first immediate intervention is intravenous calcium gluconate. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of action of calcium gluconate in hyperkalemia?
choices: Calcium raises the cardiac myocyte threshold for depolarization
Calcium shifts K+ from ECF to ICF
explanations: Correct. Hyperkalemia partially depolarizes the cardiac myocyte resting membrane potential (because the K+ Nernst equation predicts a less negative resting potential at higher [K+]e). With the resting potential closer to threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels begin to inactivate, slowing conduction. Calcium gluconate raises the threshold for depolarization, restoring the gap between resting and threshold and stabilizing electrical activity. The effect is rapid (minutes) but transient (~30 min), and calcium does NOT lower plasma K+. It is therefore combined with cellular-shift agents (insulin/glucose, β2 agonist, bicarbonate if acidotic) and K+-removal therapies (loop diuretic, GI cation exchanger, dialysis).
Incorrect. Calcium does not chemically chelate K+.
Incorrect. Calcium does not affect renal K+ excretion.
Incorrect. Calcium does not shift K+ between compartments.
Incorrect. Calcium does not affect intestinal K+ absorption.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with end-stage renal disease has K+ 7.8 with ECG changes. After IV calcium gluconate, the team gives intravenous regular insulin 10 units along with 50 mL of 50% dextrose. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which insulin lowers plasma K+ in this setting?
choices: Insulin activates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting K+ from ECF into cells
explanations: Incorrect. Insulin does not affect intestinal K+ absorption.

Correct. Insulin binds its tyrosine kinase receptor and activates Na+/K+-ATPase via PI3K/Akt and other downstream signals, accelerating Na+ extrusion and K+ uptake into cells. Plasma K+ falls within 15–30 minutes by ~0.5–1.0 mEq/L. Because total body K+ is unchanged, this is a TEMPORIZING measure — to be combined with K+-removing therapies (loop diuretic if intact kidney function, GI cation exchanger, or dialysis). Glucose (10 units of insulin + 25 g dextrose) prevents iatrogenic hypoglycemia, which is the main complication.
Incorrect. Insulin does not chemically precipitate K+.
Incorrect. Insulin does not increase renal K+ excretion.
Incorrect. Insulin does not cause osmotic diuresis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with severe hyperkalemia (K+ 7.5) is given high-dose nebulized albuterol (10–20 mg) in addition to calcium gluconate and insulin/glucose. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which β2 agonist therapy lowers plasma K+?
choices: β2-adrenergic activation of Na+/K+-ATPase shifts K+ into cells
explanations: Incorrect. β2 agonists do not principally raise renal K+ excretion.
Incorrect. β2 agonists do not affect intestinal K+ absorption.

Correct. β2-adrenergic activation stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase via Gs-coupled cAMP signaling, driving K+ from ECF into cells. Plasma K+ falls by ~0.5 mEq/L within 30 minutes. Doses used for hyperkalemia (nebulized albuterol 10–20 mg) are 4–8× higher than typical asthma doses. Limitations: ~20% of patients do not respond appreciably (so should be combined with other measures), and tachyarrhythmias may occur. The mechanism is synergistic with insulin/glucose because the two pathways converge on the same Na+/K+-ATPase pump.
Incorrect. Vasoconstriction is not the mechanism (β2 agonists are vasodilators).
Incorrect. β2 agonists do not produce osmotic diuresis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with hyperkalemia (K+ 7.0) has been treated with calcium gluconate, insulin/glucose, and nebulized albuterol — and his K+ has fallen to 6.0. The team now needs to actually REMOVE potassium from the body. Which of the following options is/are appropriate at this stage?
choices: Loop diuretic, GI cation-exchange resins, or hemodialysis
explanations: Incorrect. Calcium gluconate stabilizes the membrane but does not lower plasma K+.
Incorrect. Insulin shifts K+ into cells (temporizing) but does not remove it from the body.
Incorrect. β2 agonists shift K+ into cells (temporizing) but do not remove it.

Correct. Therapies that actually REMOVE K+ from the body include: (1) loop diuretics (if kidney function preserved) — increase distal Na+ delivery and urine flow, driving K+ excretion; (2) GI cation-exchange resins — sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate, classical but slow and constipating, with rare bowel necrosis); patiromer (newer, faster, better-tolerated); sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (Lokelma, fast onset, well-tolerated); (3) hemodialysis (the fastest definitive treatment, used in severe or refractory hyperkalemia, especially in ESRD/AKI). All address the total body K+ excess; cellular-shift therapies do not.
Incorrect. Hypertonic saline can produce some K+ shift via volume changes but is not a recognized hyperkalemia treatment.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on long-term hemodialysis presents with K+ 7.2 and peaked T waves after missing a session. After temporizing therapies (calcium gluconate, insulin/glucose), he is taken for emergent hemodialysis. Which of the following best characterizes the rate of K+ removal during HD with a low-K dialysate?
choices: Variable, but typically less than 10 mEq/hour
explanations: Correct. Hemodialysis is the most rapid and reliable means of K+ removal in severe hyperkalemia, particularly in ESRD or oliguric AKI where the kidney cannot excrete K+ and GI cation exchangers are too slow. With a low-K (1–2 mEq/L) dialysate, K+ removal of approximately 25–40 mEq/hour is typical, with most of the gradient achieved in the first 1–2 hours of treatment. Plasma K+ can rebound after HD as cellular shifts equilibrate. Important caveats: very rapid K+ correction (e.g., from 8 to 3 in one session) can precipitate arrhythmias of its own, so dialysate K+ is sometimes adjusted to avoid an excessive gradient.
Incorrect. <5 mEq/hour is far below the typical removal rate.
Incorrect. Standard HD removes K+; it does not add it.
Incorrect. While individual rates vary, typical removal is well above 10 mEq/hour during the rapid phase.
Incorrect. PD does remove K+ but more slowly; conventional HD is the standard for severe hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide develops hypokalemia (K+ 2.8) and metabolic alkalosis. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of thiazide-induced hypokalemia?
choices: Increased distal Na+ delivery, urine flow, and aldosterone activation
explanations: Incorrect. Thiazide does not directly activate the K+ pump.
Incorrect. Thiazide does not affect intestinal K+ absorption.
Incorrect. Thiazide does not affect dietary K+ losses.
Incorrect. Thiazide does not produce an inappropriate insulin spike.

Correct. Thiazide diuretics produce hypokalemia through the same cascade as loop diuretics: increased distal Na+ delivery, increased urine flow, and volume contraction-mediated RAAS activation. All three amplify distal K+ secretion at the principal cell. The accompanying metabolic alkalosis arises from increased H+ secretion at adjacent α-intercalated cells (driven by the same aldosterone). Strategies to mitigate: K+ supplementation, addition of a K+-sparing diuretic (amiloride, triamterene) or aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone), or use of combination therapy (e.g., HCTZ + amiloride).

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation and HFrEF on chronic digoxin and furosemide presents with vomiting (3 days), palpitations, and yellow-tinted vision. ECG shows ventricular bigeminy and prominent U waves. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia potentiate digoxin toxicity
Hyperkalemia is more dangerous than hypokalemia in digoxin toxicity
Digoxin level alone determines toxicity; electrolytes are irrelevant
Hypokalemia is protective in digoxin toxicity
explanations: Correct. Digoxin inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, which has two consequences: (1) intracellular Na+ rises, raising intracellular Ca2+ via Na+/Ca2+ exchange — increasing inotropy (the therapeutic effect); and (2) at high levels, the same inhibition disrupts cellular electrophysiology and produces arrhythmia. Digoxin and K+ compete at the Na+/K+-ATPase binding site: hypokalemia reduces K+ competition, allowing digoxin to bind more strongly and inhibit the pump more profoundly. Hypomagnesemia further potentiates toxicity. The classical clinical picture: vomiting, yellow-tinted vision, ventricular ectopy/bigeminy, and U waves (hypokalemia). Management: replete K+ and Mg2+, hold digoxin, IV Digibind (digoxin-specific Fab) for severe toxicity (life-threatening arrhythmia, K+ >5 in acute toxicity).

Incorrect. Hypokalemia (not hyperkalemia) potentiates chronic digoxin toxicity by reducing K+ competition at the Na+/K+-ATPase binding site. Note: ACUTE digoxin overdose produces hyperkalemia from massive pump inhibition (which IS dangerous), but chronic toxicity is potentiated by hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Electrolytes — particularly K+ and Mg2+ — strongly modulate digoxin toxicity at any given drug level.
Incorrect. Hypokalemia worsens (not improves) digoxin toxicity.
Incorrect. Hypocalcemia does not principally precipitate digoxin toxicity; if anything, hypercalcemia worsens digoxin toxicity (because both raise intracellular Ca2+).

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is admitted in DKA with plasma K+ 5.4 mEq/L. He is started on IV insulin and isotonic saline. After 4 hours, plasma K+ has fallen to 3.4 mEq/L. He has had no significant urinary K+ losses in the interval. Compared with pre-treatment values, which row in the table best describes the changes in K+ distribution and total body K+ during insulin therapy?
explanations: Incorrect. Insulin LOWERS plasma K+; intracellular K+ RISES with redistribution.

Correct. Insulin activates Na+/K+-ATPase via tyrosine kinase signaling, driving K+ from ECF into cells (predominantly skeletal muscle and liver). Plasma K+ falls and intracellular K+ rises through redistribution. Total body K+ is essentially UNCHANGED in the short term — the K+ has simply moved between compartments. (Note: in DKA, total body K+ is depleted from prior osmotic diuresis, but the ongoing renal K+ losses are slower than the insulin-driven shift, so over 4 hours total body K+ has not changed appreciably.) For this reason, K+ supplementation is added to DKA fluids when plasma K+ falls below ~5.0, to anticipate the cellular shift.
Incorrect. Insulin causes a NET shift INTO cells, lowering plasma K+; total body K+ does not increase.
Incorrect. Intracellular K+ does not fall during insulin therapy; it rises as K+ shifts in.
Incorrect. Insulin produces a measurable K+ shift within 15–30 minutes; values do not remain unchanged.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a serum K+ of 2.8 mEq/L and is symptomatic with weakness. She is to receive intravenous KCl. Which of the following best characterizes the recommended rate and route of K+ replacement?
choices: 10–20 mEq/hour peripheral IV (up to 40 with central line)
As fast as tolerated; no upper limit
explanations: Incorrect. IV bolus of K+ at this dose would produce dangerous transient hyperkalemia and arrhythmia.
Incorrect. 100 mEq/hour is far too rapid and risks lethal arrhythmia.

Correct. Standard IV KCl replacement: ≤10 mEq/hour by peripheral IV (concentration ≤40 mEq/L to avoid vein irritation); up to 20 mEq/hour by peripheral IV with cardiac monitoring; up to 40 mEq/hour by central line with continuous monitoring (reserved for severe symptomatic hypokalemia or critical illness). Faster rates risk transient hyperkalemia, painful infusion, and arrhythmia. Oral KCl is preferred when possible (40 mEq doses, repeat every 4–6 hours). Concurrent Mg+ replacement is important — refractory hypokalemia often reflects Mg2+ deficiency.
Incorrect. 1 mEq/hour is too slow to correct symptomatic hypokalemia.
Incorrect. There IS an upper limit; exceeding it risks life-threatening hyperkalemia and arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic ulcerative colitis–related diarrhea has serum K+ 2.7 despite IV KCl 40 mEq six hours ago. Repeat serum Mg2+ is 1.2 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Increase the KCl dose without addressing magnesium
Replenish magnesium with IV magnesium sulfate
explanations: Incorrect. K+ replacement without Mg2+ correction will remain ineffective because of ongoing inappropriate renal K+ wasting.
Incorrect. Calcium does not address hypomagnesemia and is not the issue here.
Incorrect. While potassium phosphate is sometimes used (e.g., in DKA with concurrent hypophosphatemia), it does not address the underlying Mg2+ deficiency.

Correct. ROMK channels in collecting duct principal cells are normally closed by intracellular Mg2+ binding to the inner pore. In hypomagnesemia, this 'Mg2+ block' is lost, and ROMK remains inappropriately open even when plasma K+ is low — driving ongoing renal K+ wasting. K+ replacement is therefore offset by losses. Replenishing magnesium first (IV magnesium sulfate, e.g., 2–4 g over 2 hours) restores ROMK closure and allows K+ stores to rebuild. In chronic GI losses, both K+ and Mg2+ are commonly depleted.
Incorrect. The patient has symptomatic hypokalemia; discontinuing supplementation would be inappropriate.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old patient with DKA has plasma K+ 5.5 mEq/L on admission and is known to be total-body K+ depleted from osmotic diuresis. After 24 hours of insulin and IVF (with K+ added when plasma K+ fell below 5.0), plasma K+ is 3.8 mEq/L despite ongoing K+ supplementation. Which of the following best describes the relationship between plasma K+ and total body K+?
choices: Plasma K+ always reflects total body K+
Plasma K+ depends solely on dietary K+ intake
Plasma K+ is independent of cellular shifts
Plasma K+ reflects ECF only and shifts independent of total body K+
Plasma K+ is fixed by aldosterone alone, regardless of total body K+
explanations: Incorrect. Plasma K+ is a poor index of total body K+. Cellular shifts (insulin, β2 stimulation, acid-base, aldosterone, cell lysis) can produce large plasma K+ changes without commensurate change in total body K+.
Incorrect. Plasma K+ depends on intake, cellular distribution, and renal/GI excretion — not on intake alone.
Incorrect. Plasma K+ is highly dependent on cellular shifts (the dominant mechanism for minute-to-minute changes).

Correct. Plasma K+ measures only the ~2% of total body K+ that resides in the ECF. Cellular shifts (insulin, β2 agonists, acid-base, aldosterone, cell lysis) and renal/GI excretion both contribute. In DKA, insulin deficiency and acidosis transiently shift K+ out of cells, producing apparent normokalemia or hyperkalemia DESPITE substantial total body K+ depletion from osmotic diuresis. Insulin therapy reverses the shift, revealing the hidden deficit and frequently producing hypokalemia by 4–12 hours unless K+ is actively repleted. This is why K+ supplementation is initiated when plasma K+ falls below ~5.0 in DKA management.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is one (slow) regulator of renal K+ excretion, but plasma K+ is set in the moment principally by cellular shifts.
